content: Hypopigmentation refers to the loss of skin color, which occurs due to either a depletion of melanocytes or a reduction in the amino acid tyrosine, a critical substrate used by melanocytes to produce melanin. Causes of Hypopigmentation: 1. Common Conditions: Pityriasis Alba: Frequently seen in children with atopy, presenting as hypopigmented patches with fine scaling. Lesions retain some pigment and are less sharply demarcated. Post-inflammatory Hypopigmentation: Occurs after skin inflammation or injury. Tinea Versicolor: A fungal infection that may cause vitiligo-like changes, often after treatment. Diagnosis is aided by the presence of fine scaling, positive potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation, and distribution primarily on the trunk and neck. Halo Nevus: A mole surrounded by a depigmented halo, often associated with immune activity. Tuberous Sclerosis: Characterized by hypopigmented macules, shagreen patches, angiofibromas, and periungual fibromas, often with neurological sequelae. Albinism: A genetic condition marked by a complete or partial lack of melanin production. 2. Drug-Induced Hypopigmentation: Certain medications, such as corticosteroids (e.g., clocortolone pivalate, desoximetasone, dexamethasone, fluocinolone acetonide) and retinoids, can lead to hypopigmentation. 3. Autoimmune Disorders: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada Syndrome: An autoimmune condition involving bilateral uveitis, auditory and neurological symptoms, and cutaneous depigmentation due to T-cell-mediated destruction of melanin-containing tissues. 4. Infections: Tuberculoid Leprosy: Presents as hypochromic patches with reduced sensation to light touch. Pinta: A treponemal infection causing hypopigmented lesions. Onchocerciasis: A parasitic infection that may result in skin depigmentation. 5. Genetic Syndromes: Incontinentia Pigmenti Achromians (Hypomelanosis of Ito): Characterized by hypopigmented whorls, streaks, and patches along Blaschko's lines, often associated with neurological, skeletal, and ocular abnormalities. Waardenburg Syndrome: Features include a white forelock, hypertelorism, and variable deafness, sometimes linked to congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease). Piebaldism: Presents with a white forelock, midline depigmentation of the anterior body, and bilateral shin depigmentation, inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Menkes Syndrome: An X-linked recessive disorder with diffuse hair and body hypopigmentation, accompanied by neurodegenerative changes. 6. Other Conditions: Post-traumatic Leukoderma: Occurs after deep burns or scarring that destroys melanocyte precursors in the bulge area of hair follicles. It can be challenging to distinguish from true vitiligo when scarring is not apparent. Neoplasia: Halo Nevus: Depigmentation around a cutaneous melanoma (malignant Sutton’s phenomenon) or more widespread vitiligoid changes. Mycosis Fungoides: A type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma that may present with depigmentation, particularly in dark-skinned individuals. Diagnosis often requires a biopsy. Idiopathic Causes: Acquired Macular Hypomelanosis: Common in young adults, presenting as white macules on the trunk, especially the lower back and axillae. Propionibacterium acnes is a suspected cause. Idiopathic Guttate Hypomelanosis: Small hypopigmented macules (≤5 mm) in a photodistribution pattern, often on sun-damaged skin of the arms and legs. Malformations: Nevus Anemicus: A congenital vascular anomaly that appears hypopigmented due to reduced blood flow. Nevus Depigmentosus: A stable, non-progressive hypopigmented lesion present from birth. Chemically-Induced Leukoderma: Caused by exposure to certain chemicals (e.g., phenols, catechols) that destroy melanocytes. Lesions often have bizarre borders, scaling, and a confetti-like distribution, sometimes accompanied by pruritus. Diagnostic Considerations: A thorough history, including medication use, toxin exposure, and family history, is essential. Physical examination should assess lesion distribution, scaling, and associated features. Diagnostic tools such as Wood’s lamp examination, KOH preparation, and skin biopsy may aid in differentiating causes of hypopigmentation.
